value.reason: Hot Takes for the completed Y96 season
value.intro: Philadelphia won again, and then its two pillars walked away. The voters made a mess of the awards, the market chased the wrong Eagles, and a record fell in Cincinnati that nobody rewarded. The arguments are ours; the figures are the league's.

takes.headline: Grover Calitro Set the League Record With 43 Rushing Touchdowns and Lost Offensive Player of the Year. Indefensible.
takes.dek: Calitro: 1,904 yards and 43 scores. The winner, Alton Yeldon: 1,558 yards and 27.
body: No back in the tracked history of this league has scored 43 rushing touchdowns in a season. Siran Spector's 42 in Y89 was the mark, and Calitro went past it while carrying Cincinnati to the Super Bowl. He ran for 1,904 yards, 346 more than Alton Yeldon, and scored 16 more touchdowns. Yeldon took the trophy home to Seattle anyway.

There is no reading of the numbers that makes this vote right. Calitro was the best offensive player outside Philadelphia and arguably the best inside it too. The Bengals lost the final 40-26, and his card still costs 189. The voters will not get a cleaner chance to be correct, and they missed it.

takes.headline: Ryland Maxwell Retired 4 Touchdowns Short of Second Place. The Greatest Ever Left Too Early.
takes.dek: 2,574 yards and 25 touchdowns in his last season, and 421 career rushing scores to Lane McCoy's 458.
body: Nobody retires after a 2,574-yard season. Maxwell did, at 34, after playing all 21 of Philadelphia's games and collecting his seventh Super Bowl MVP and 13th ring. He owns the career rushing yards record at 32,108, and his Career Legacy of 14,903 is the highest in the league.

But the touchdown list tells a different story. Lane McCoy scored 458 rushing touchdowns, Siran Spector 425, Maxwell 421. That is 4 short of second place and 37 short of first, a gap one more ordinary Maxwell season would have closed. The greatest running back the league has seen walked away with a number still on the table, and the record book will carry that asterisk for good.

takes.headline: Margus Leglue's MVP Corrected Last Year's Mistake: 41 Touchdowns and 1 Interception Beats 52 and 17
takes.dek: Bones Crawford threw more touchdowns. Leglue threw 16 fewer interceptions, and the voters finally weighed both.
body: Last year this column argued that Bones Crawford's interceptions should have cost him the MVP. They did not. This year they did, and the voters were right. Crawford threw for 4,339 yards and 52 touchdowns with 17 interceptions. Leglue threw for 3,803 yards and 41 touchdowns and was picked off once.

Leglue is 36, has been a Lion since Y80 as far as the record shows, has never won a ring, and had never won this award. His card went from 237 to 874, a 269% jump that still prices him like a role player. Crawford plays with the best supporting cast in football. Leglue made Detroit go by himself. That is what most valuable means.

takes.headline: Bones Crawford's Card Rose 124% in the Year He Lost the MVP. The Market Is Buying a Retirement.
takes.dek: From 8,559 to 19,210 after a season with 17 interceptions, 7 more than the year before.
body: Crawford was the Y95 MVP with 10 interceptions. In Y96 he threw 17, lost the award to a Detroit quarterback, and watched his card climb from 8,559 to 19,210. That is not a market rewarding a season. That is a market pricing in the fact that Ryland Maxwell and Akiem Brock are gone and somebody in Philadelphia has to be the face of the club.

He has 5 MVPs and 8 rings, and the Hall of Fame watch already scores him at 73, above the bar of 65. The case is real. But a quarterback whose interceptions rose by 7 just lost the two best players he ever stood behind. Buyers at 19,210 are paying for the dynasty, not for the passer.

takes.headline: A.T. Hoyer Matched the Defensive Player of the Year's 237 Tackles in 3 Fewer Games
takes.dek: Abraham Jack needed 20 games for his 237. Hoyer got there in 17, with one more interception.
body: Abraham Jack is a deserving name on a trophy. He is not the most deserving one. Jack made 237 tackles and 2 interceptions across Buffalo's 20 games. A.T. Hoyer made 237 tackles and 3 interceptions in the Raiders' 17. Per game that is 13.94 tackles for Hoyer and 11.85 for Jack, and it is not close.

The voters rewarded the playoff run, not the player. Hoyer has made 2,911 career tackles without this award, and his card nearly doubling to 5,523 says the market saw what the ballot did not. Jack's own card went to 435. One of these players is a star, and it is the one who stayed home in January.

takes.headline: Jacob Proise's Card Is Up 398% on 786 Yards. Sell It Before Everyone Else Does.
takes.dek: The tight end went from 1,109 to 5,527 while the receiver beside him gained 2,096 yards and 26%.
body: Proise had a good season: 51 catches, 786 yards and 14 touchdowns in all 21 of Philadelphia's games, and his rating jumped from 84 to 93. The market treated it like a coronation, pushing his card from 1,109 to 5,527.

Now look one locker over. Calvin Wingo II caught 104 passes for 2,096 yards and 18 touchdowns on the same offense, and his card rose 26%. Proise is a fine tight end on a team that just lost its running back of record, and that rating bump is real. A 398% rise for half of Wingo's production is not a valuation. It is a bubble, and bubbles pop the moment the ring count stops climbing.

takes.headline: Ty Lock Threw for 68,237 Yards and the Hall of Fame Said No. The Hall Got It Right.
takes.dek: 2 rings, both with the Jets, then a Giants career from Y83 to Y95 without another.
body: Lock's first ballot came and went, and the outrage is already loud. It should not be. He threw for 68,237 yards and 627 touchdowns, and he also threw 137 interceptions. His 2 MVPs and 2 rings are real, but both rings came with the Jets, and the Giants won nothing with him from Y83 through Y95.

Measure him against the real standard. Sherman Brandson threw for 91,463 yards. Bones Crawford, whom this column called the better quarterback 3 seasons ago, already has 5 MVPs and 8 rings. Lock was very good for a very long time. The Hall exists for the players who were the best, and he never was.

takes.headline: Six Straight Titles, and the 13-4 Eagles Were the Weakest Champion of the Run
takes.dek: 4 losses, the most since Philadelphia hired Dorren Skura, and still nobody could finish the job.
body: The Eagles went 17-0 in Y95. They went 13-4 in Y96, their most losses since Skura arrived in Y88, and then won the Super Bowl 40-26 over Cincinnati for a 6th straight title anyway. That is the indictment, and it is not of Philadelphia.

Every contender saw a beatable Eagles team this year and none of them could do it in January. The Bengals had the league's record-setting runner and still lost by double digits. Now Ryland Maxwell and Akiem Brock are retired, and the excuses run out. If the rest of the league cannot dethrone a club that just lost its two Hall of Famers, it does not deserve to.

takes.headline: Jamon Brooker Just Tied the Career Interceptions Record. He Is the Best Player Without a Ring.
takes.dek: 43 interceptions, level with Hall of Famer Damar Hobbs, 2 Defensive Player of the Year awards and a Hall of Fame watch score of 91.
body: Brooker made 186 tackles and 2 interceptions for Green Bay this season, which took him to 43 for his career and level with Damar Hobbs for the league record. Hobbs is in the Hall of Fame. Brooker will be too: the watch already scores him at 91, the highest of any active player, with 2 Defensive Player of the Year awards behind it.

What he does not have is a ring, and at 33 the window is narrowing. Philadelphia hoards them. The best defender of his generation is spending his prime in the wrong building, and whoever trades for him first will be buying the last missing piece of a Hall of Fame career.

stats.label: Defensive Player of the Year awards

takes.headline: Akiem Brock Went In First Ballot Without a Single Award, and That Is the Hall Working
takes.dek: 8 rings, 181 games, and the highest Career Legacy of any offensive lineman.
body: Offensive linemen rarely collect trophies, and Brock never won an individual award. What he won was 8 rings, every one of them in Philadelphia, across 181 games. His Career Legacy of 11,394 ranks first among offensive linemen, and the ballot scored him at 79, comfortably clear of the bar of 65.

This is the Hall of Fame doing its job. A trophy-count Hall would have left him waiting behind running backs and quarterbacks with shinier shelves. Instead Brock goes in beside Ryland Maxwell, the back he blocked for, which is exactly where he belongs. Maxwell got the yards. Brock was the reason there was room to get them.

value.intro: Y95 ended the way the last four did, with Philadelphia lifting the trophy. Beneath the parade sat a lucky contender, a ringless runner and a star receiver who learned what life outside the Eagles looks like. The arguments are ours to defend; the figures come straight from the league data.

takes.headline: Ryland Maxwell Has Passed Sherman Brandson. Stop Calling It a Debate.
takes.dek: Career Legacy 14,019 to 13,540, 12 rings to 10, and both career rushing records.
body: A year ago this column said one more ordinary season would settle it. Maxwell did not have an ordinary season. He ran for 2,141 yards and 30 touchdowns, pushed the career rushing marks to 29,534 yards and 396 touchdowns, and was named Super Bowl MVP for the sixth time. His Career Legacy climbed to 14,019, 479 clear of Brandson's 13,540.

He did it at 33, and he did it in 18 of the Eagles' 20 games; injury cost him the other 2. Brandson still owns the passing book and 8 MVPs. Maxwell owns 12 rings to Brandson's 10, the rushing book and now the top of the list. The greatest player in league history is a running back, and the argument is over.

takes.headline: Keenan Viennes Was a Philadelphia Product, and the Jets Found Out the Hard Way
takes.dek: From 2,041 yards as Offensive Player of the Year to 726 in New York.
body: A year ago Viennes won Offensive Player of the Year in an Eagles uniform with 2,041 receiving yards. In Y95 he played all 17 games for the Jets and caught 82 passes for 726 yards, 8.9 a catch. Same player, a full season, about a third of the yardage.

The strange part is the card. His OVR rose from 79 to 82 and his card value more than doubled, from 160 to 361. The market priced the name. The field priced the system he left. The Jets finished 5-11-1 and lost to Philadelphia 35-19, while Calvin Wingo II stayed behind and won the award Viennes had held. Some receivers make an offense. Viennes, it turns out, was made by one.

takes.headline: Calvin Wingo II Won Offensive Player of the Year With Ryland Maxwell's Touchdowns
takes.dek: Maxwell's touchdown catches fell from 53 to 7; Wingo's touchdowns rose from 7 to 25.
body: Wingo was very good in Y95: 114 catches, 2,267 yards and 25 touchdowns in 20 games. He was also very good in Y94, when he gained 1,994 yards and scored 7 times. The yardage barely moved. The touchdowns more than tripled.

They came from somewhere. In Y94 Maxwell caught 53 touchdown passes; in Y95 he caught 7. Bones Crawford stopped flipping the ball to his running back near the goal line and started finding his receiver instead. That is a play-calling story, not a breakout. Wingo is a fine receiver, and his card says so. Offensive Player of the Year, though, went to the man standing where the ball was sent.

takes.headline: Bones Crawford Halved His Interceptions and Still Threw More Than Anyone. That Is Not an MVP Season.
takes.dek: 10 interceptions, 3 more than any other passer, and fewer yards than a 39-year-old Patriot.
body: Credit where due: last year this column called Crawford careless for 20 interceptions, and he cut them to 10. That still led the league; Sione Garland of the Broncos was next with 7. And Dustin Milton of the Patriots, at 39, threw for 4,319 yards to Crawford's 4,271.

Crawford's case is 52 touchdown passes and a 17-0 club. Fine. But his touchdown passes fell from 68, injury cost him 2 of the Eagles' 20 games, and his top receiver piled up 2,267 yards. The MVP rewarded the best team, not the best season. Ryland Maxwell or Calvin Wingo II had the stronger claim, and Milton had the better arm year.

takes.headline: We Said Dallas Had Philadelphia's Number. Dallas Went 2-15. The Rivalry Is Dead.
takes.dek: The worst record in the league, 0-8 at home, and two more losses to the Eagles.
body: Last year this column called the Cowboys the only club that knew how to beat Philadelphia. That aged badly. Dallas finished 2-15, last in the league's power table, winless at home at 0-8 and outscored by 200 points.

The Eagles beat them twice, 32-27 in Dallas and 40-22 in Philadelphia, and the series now stands 12-3-1 in Philadelphia's favour. A rivalry needs two sides that can win. The Giants took the Eagles to the final snap in a one-point game. The Commanders went 12-5. Dallas is a fixture on the schedule now, not a rival, and this column regrets the error.

takes.headline: The 14-3 Ravens Were the Luckiest Team in Football
takes.dek: A plus-54 point margin, 10-1 in one-score games and about 9.5 wins' worth of football.
body: Baltimore won 14 games and outscored opponents by 54 points. The Chiefs outscored theirs by 142, and the Buccaneers by 124 while winning only 10. The difference is close games: the Ravens went 10-1 in one-score games, and nobody repeats that on purpose.

By points scored and allowed, the Ravens played like a 9.5-win team, which leaves 4.5 wins of luck, the most in the league. They gave up 31.8 points a game. That is not a contender's defense. Enjoy the 14-3, Baltimore. Next season the close ones start landing the other way.

takes.headline: Maurice Vigil Outscored Ryland Maxwell on the Ground, and Nobody Outside Kansas City Noticed
takes.dek: 34 rushing touchdowns to Maxwell's 30, the most in the league, at 34 years old.
body: Maxwell took the career records and the headlines. The league's best goal-line runner in Y95 wore red. Vigil scored 34 rushing touchdowns in 20 games, more than anyone, and added 1,755 yards for a Chiefs club that went 15-2 and reached Super Bowl CLIV.

There it ended, 24-19, and that is the rest of the Vigil story: 352 career rushing touchdowns, a Chief since Y82 as far as the record shows, and no ring. The Chiefs also lost to the 6-11 Raiders, the upset of the season, and Skura's clubs are now 5-0 against them all time. Vigil deserved a better club. Kansas City deserved a better ending for him.

takes.headline: Travon Swaim's Defensive Player of the Year Was a Lifetime Award, and He Earned It
takes.dek: 249 games for Detroit, a first trophy at 34, and a card that more than doubled.
body: Isaiah Pinkney of the Ravens made 238 tackles in Y95 and Swaim made 232, so this was no runaway on the numbers. It did not need to be. Swaim has played 249 games, a Lion since Y81 as far as the record shows, and his 2,865 career tackles had never brought him this award.

At 34 he played 20 games, made 232 tackles and 3 interceptions, and the market finally caught up: his card value went from 2,459 to 5,983. Detroit won its division at 9-8 and lost to the Eagles 30-16 in the conference round. The voters picked the career. This time the career was the right answer.

takes.headline: The Buccaneers Were the Second-Best Team in the NFC, Whatever 10-7 Says
takes.dek: Plus-124 in points, 3-6 in one-score games, about 10.8 wins' worth of football.
body: Tampa Bay outscored opponents by 124 points, the best margin in the NFC outside Philadelphia, and finished 10-7, second in its own division behind an 11-6 Falcons club that was plus-17. The gap is close games: the Buccaneers went 3-6 in one-score games.

By points they played like a 10.8-win team. Then they drew the Eagles in the divisional round and lost 40-10, so nobody will remember this club. They should. Swap the luck with Baltimore and Tampa Bay is the team everyone calls Philadelphia's heir.

takes.headline: Five Straight Titles, 17-0 and a 298-Point Margin: Philadelphia Has Broken the League
takes.dek: The best offense and the best defense in Y95, and only one Eagles game all year decided by a single point.
body: Super Bowl CLIV was the Eagles' fifth title in a row, and the closest anyone came all season was the Giants, who lost 32-31. Philadelphia scored 36.7 points a game and allowed 19.2, both the best in the league, and went 17-0 for the second time in three seasons.

The game tries to stop this. Its draft rule caps each class by the last record, and after a perfect season the best prospects in the Y96 class top out at 6 half-stars. It has not mattered. The Chiefs went 15-2, the best record anyone else managed, and still lost the final by 5. The rest of the league is playing for second place, and second place is not close.
